title: You can trust the build and still miss the change
summary: A loop that produces working software has only solved the output. I write the behavior that should change before an assistant drafts, and a missing sentence keeps the piece off the approval list.

## The question

A sloppy draft used to be the failure I watched for. I thought a tighter specification would pull a wandering assistant back, and that the result would then be safe to keep. Yuval Yeret, in [From Vibe Coding to Developing the Company](https://www.scrum.org/resources/blog/vibe-coding-developing-company), treats that hope as the early stage rather than the fix. He describes the loose way of building as a slot machine attached to a studio tour: a front you can walk through, little behind the wall, fine for a look and a poor way to make something a team will have to live with.

People answer that looseness with a specification, then with policies and handoffs, so the loop feels less like a gamble. His claim starts after that answer. A loop you have learned to trust still produces output. A build that runs is not yet a change in what someone does when they sit down on Monday.

The slice I can check is the essay in front of me. Orbit is the site where these pieces are published. An assistant may draft one. I can still require that the behavior is named before any paragraph is written.

## The issue

The issue is a finished draft that looks ready to approve, while the change it was supposed to cause was never written down.

Yeret's claim is that the feature you specify is not the outcome that feature was meant to move, and a release still does not show whether anyone's behavior changed. I am keeping that split and leaving his workshop in his essay. He goes on to the kits he would install and the metric loop he would run after deployment. I have not run those steps, so I will not describe them as a result I have checked. He does say, and this part I am using, that a person still decides whether the intent itself should change or whether a larger bet is worth funding. Most of the organizations he has worked with call the teams product teams and still pass features across handoffs. An assistant that is free to choose the work before the outcome is clear will build something that functions and does not matter.

Trustworthy output is still output.

The person who loses is the reader holding a polished piece and no rule they can use, and the author who spent the review on sentences when the missing line was the behavior.

## The sentence that can be wrong

On a weekly essay I already refuse to start the prose until two lines can stand without the article beside them. One line is the issue, the sentence a stranger could repeat. The other is the gate, the check I already run on this draft so the same miss does not ship again. When those lines only retell the source's demo, I throw them out, and the assistant does not receive a document to finish.

That is a smaller practice than the loop he wants after deployment. I am not asking an assistant to watch whether last week's essay changed anyone's week. I have not measured that. A published piece is not evidence that a reader did anything differently, and I will not pretend otherwise. What I can refuse on this Monday is the approval step, when I still cannot say the behavior.

The sentence has to be one that could turn out false. A line like "make the work more useful" would let every draft through, which means it is not a gate. This week the sentence is narrow. Name the behavior before the build. If that name is missing, the draft stays unpublished. I still publish by approving the draft, and I can leave it sitting. That approval is the wrong moment to invent the behavior, because by then the prose is already arguing, and I am defending a candidate instead of deciding whether it had a point.

The move fails when I write a sentence that has the shape of a behavior and still fits whatever topic I happened to open. Then the gate is a label. An assistant will draft under a label without complaining. I have not gone back through older essays to count how often the opening sentence was that kind of label. Until I have, the rule stays on this artifact. The notes come first. A missing behavior keeps the essay off the approval list.

He also says the same trouble gets worse once you leave the software team, and that a person who builds software can help other people work on the way the work is done, rather than sit beside each task. I have not tried that with anyone else's job, so I will not offer it as a method. The rule I will keep is the one on this draft.

## Takeaway

A loop you trust has finished a build. It has not named the change. I write the behavior before any draft exists, in a sentence that could be false. If I cannot write that sentence, the piece stays a draft.
